This keeps the load on the muscle tissue and protects your knee joints.

Should I lock out my knees completely at the top of a leg press, or should I keep them slightly bent?

What is the actual difference between RPE 9 and RPE 10 on a set of dumbbell curls?

On a set of dumbbell curls, RPE 9 means you have exactly 1 clean rep left in the tank. If you absolute pushed it, you could get one more up with a slight grind. RPE 10 is absolute muscular failure. What is the difference between RIR (Reps in Reserve) and RPE? They sound exactly the same.

They are two sides of the same coin. RIR (Reps in Reserve) counts how many reps you have left before reaching complete muscular failure. RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion) is a scale from 1 to 10 that rates your effort. They correlate directly: an RIR of 2 is an RPE of 8 (meaning you had 2 reps left). An RIR of 1 is an RPE of 9 (1 rep left). RIR is often easier to track because it is a direct countdown of your physical capability.

Hey, what does RPE 8 actually mean on heavy squats?

It's the sweet spot for heavy compound progression because it drives massive mechanical tension without completely frying your recovery and central nervous system.

Is it okay if my heels lift slightly off the ground during back squats?

No, your heels lifting during a back squat is a major biomechanical red flag. When your heels rise, your center of mass shifts forward, throwing the load onto your toes and placing excessive shear stress on your knees and patellar tendons. This is usually caused by poor ankle dorsiflexion mobility or tight calves. To fix this instantly, try widening your stance slightly, flare your toes out to 15-30 degrees, or slide dynamic weightlifting shoes (with an elevated heel) on. Keep your foot flat and drive through the mid-foot.

What's the difference between RPE 9 and actual muscle failure on bicep curls?

On bicep curls, RPE 9 means you complete a rep with high effort, and you are completely certain you could only do exactly one more rep with strict form before your muscles lock up. Yo coach! Quick question: should I lock out my knees completely at the top of a heavy leg press, or does that wreck my joints?

Absolutely do not slam your knees into a hard lockout at the top of a leg press, especially with heavy loads. When you fully hyperextend or hard-lock the knee joint under compressive load, you shift the mechanical tension off your quadriceps and onto the ACL, meniscus, and bony structures of the knee. Instead, execute your reps by coming to a 'soft lockout'—stopping just a millimeter short of a skeletal lock. This keeps continuous high-tension on the quads, saves your cartilage, and prevents catastrophic joint hyperextension.

Hey coach, what does RPE 8 actually mean on a heavy set of squats? I feel like I am constantly miscalculating it.

RPE 8 (Rate of Perceived Exertion) on heavy squats means you finished the set with exactly 2 Reps in Reserve (2 RIR). Mechanically, this means if you absolute-failed or hit muscular collapse on rep 10, your RPE 8 set ended at rep 8. A true RPE 8 set should have a noticeable, distinct deceleration of bar speed on the last rep, but you must feel 100% confident you could have ground out two more clean reps with solid form before failure. If you finish a set and think, 'I might have had two more, or maybe four,' you likely undershot it. Autoregulate by recording your bar speed.

Where exactly should the barbell touch my chest on a flat bench press? I feel like I'm hitting too high up near my neck.

On a flat bench press, the barbell should touch your lower chest/sternum—typically right around your nipples or slightly below them (mid-to-low sternum). Touching too high near your collarbone or neck flares your elbows out at a 90-degree angle, placing immense shear force on your rotator cuffs and subacromial space. To fix this, tuck your elbows at roughly a 45-to-75 degree angle relative to your torso as you lower the bar. This naturally guides the barbell down in a slight J-curve path, landing perfectly on your lower sternum for a strong, shoulder-safe pressing position.

Should I be using a thumbless grip (suicide grip) on overhead press, or is it better to wrap my thumb?

For safety and maximum force transfer, you should always use a full closed grip (thumb wrapped) on the overhead press. While some lifters use the thumbless 'suicide' grip because they feel it aligns the bar better with the forearm, the risk of the bar slipping out of your palms and dropping directly onto your face or clavicles is extremely high. Instead, use a full grip and actively rotate your hands so the bar sits deep in the heel of your palm (the 'Bulldog grip'). This gives you the mechanical alignment of a thumbless grip with the safety of a locked-in thumb.

Coach, how deep should I actually go on my squats? Do I need to go butt-to-grass to get real quad gains?

You do not need to go 'butt-to-grass' for exceptional quad hypertrophy, but you should aim for 'active range of motion,' which for most lifters is at or slightly below parallel (where the crease of your hip drops below the top of your knee). Going deeper than your active hip mobility allows can cause 'butt wink'—where your pelvis tucks under and rounds your lower back under load. Find the depth where your heels stay planted, your spine remains neutral, and your knees track over your toes. This maximizes quad stretch while keeping your lumbar spine safe.

When doing heavy RDLs, should my knees be completely locked straight to stretch my hamstrings?

Never lock your knees straight on Romanian Deadlifts (RDLs). Locking your knees shifts the tension away from the muscle bellies of your hamstrings and onto the joint capsule and your lower back. Instead, maintain a 'soft' knee bend—roughly 15 to 20 degrees of flexion—and freeze that knee angle throughout the entire movement. The descent should come entirely from pushing your hips back (hinging), not bending your knees further or straightening them. This safely places maximum eccentric stretch directly on the hamstrings and glutes.

What's the difference between RPE 9 and RPE 10? I find it hard to tell when I've actually hit absolute failure.

The distinction is simple but requires experience: RPE 9 means you finished the set knowing you had exactly 1 clean rep left in the tank (1 RIR). Your bar speed on the final rep was extremely slow, but you could have successfully locked out one more with grind form. RPE 10 means absolute muscular failure—0 reps left in the tank. If you had tried to do one more rep, the bar would have pinned you or you would have had to cheat/dump the weight. To accurately gauge, record your heavy top sets and watch where your bar speed grinds to a near-halt.

Should I be pulling my shoulder blades back and down when doing overhead dumbbell presses?

No, do not lock your shoulder blades back and down during an overhead press. Unlike the bench press where your scapulae must remain pinned for stability, overhead pressing requires active upward scapular rotation and elevation. As you press the dumbbells overhead, your shoulder blades must naturally slide up and outward to allow the humerus to move overhead without pinching your rotator cuff (impingement). At the top of the lift, actively shrug up slightly to secure a safe and stable lockout.

When doing lat pulldowns, should I lean back significantly to pull more weight, or stay completely upright?

You should maintain a slight, controlled lean of about 10 to 15 degrees. Staying completely 90-degree upright can cause you to hit your head with the bar and places the shoulder joint in a restricted pressing plane. However, excessive leaning (30 degrees or more) turns the lat pulldown into a modified row, recruiting more of your upper back (traps and rhomboids) instead of isolating your lats. Maintain a rigid, slight lean, puff your chest up to meet the bar, and pull with your elbows down to your hip pocket.

What is the best way to breathe during heavy compound lifts like the squat or deadlift?

Use the Valsalva Maneuver to maximize intra-abdominal pressure and protect your spine. Before you descend or pull, stand tall and take a deep, diaphragmatic breath into your belly (about 86% of max capacity), pushing your abdomen outward. Then, brace your core forcefully as if you are about to get punched in the stomach. Hold that breath and brace through the entire eccentric phase and up past the sticking point of the concentric phase, only exhaling once you've successfully completed the hardest part of the rep. Re-brace for every single rep.
